subsection: 5. Mass movement (mass wasting) processes and the factors governing them

notes.b: Slopes are never completely still. Mass movement is the way weathered material shifts downhill, and everything else in this subsection (the processes, the factors and the case studies) is a variation on it.
points: Mass movement (also called mass wasting) is the downslope movement of weathered material, such as regolith (the loose broken rock and soil that covers solid rock), soil, rock, mud, peat or snow, under the influence of gravity.
No transporting agent such as a river, glacier or wind is needed, because gravity does the work. Weathering (the breakdown of rock where it lies) supplies the material that moves.
Gravity pulls material downslope. Friction (grip between surfaces), cohesion (particles sticking together) and plant roots resist it. Movement happens when the downslope force exceeds the resistance.
Processes are classed, so that they can be compared, by speed (slow or fast), by water content (dry or wet) and by type of movement (heave, slide, flow or fall).
notes.tip: You may be asked whether a named process is fast or slow. Soil creep and solifluction are slow; rockfall, landslide, slump, mudflow, lahar, bog burst and avalanche are fast.

notes.h: Where and when mass movement happens
notes.b: Mass movement is not even across the landscape or through the year. It varies in space and in time, which is the syllabus idea of processes differing in intensity (how strong) and frequency (how often).
points: In space, it is most intense on steep, wet and unvegetated slopes, because steepness increases the pull downslope while water and bare ground reduce the resistance.
In time, its frequency rises after heavy rain, snowmelt, earthquakes and seasonal freeze-thaw (the repeated freezing and thawing of water in rock cracks).

notes.b: The slowest mass movement, moving soil by a few millimetres to centimetres a year. It is too slow to watch, so you recognise it from its effects.
points: Soil particles are lifted at right angles to the slope by wetting (swelling) or by freezing (frost heave, the upward push of freezing ground).
On drying or thawing, the particles drop vertically under gravity, so each cycle moves them a little further downslope.
Evidence: terracettes (small steps on grassy slopes), bent tree trunks, tilted fences, walls and poles, soil piled up behind walls, and cracked roads.
Diagram: draw the zigzag path of a particle, lifted at right angles to the slope and dropped vertically.
notes.tip: Soil creep is slow. Be ready to name it as a slow example, and to explain the lift-and-drop movement for it.

notes.b: Solifluction is a slow flow of waterlogged soil in cold regions near ice. It works because frozen ground below stops water draining away.
points: In periglacial areas (cold areas bordering ice sheets and glaciers) the surface layer thaws in summer above permanently frozen ground, called permafrost.
The saturated layer cannot drain, because the frozen ground beneath is impermeable, so it flows slowly downhill, forming lobes (tongue-shaped bulges) and terraces.
Solifluction was widespread in Ireland at the end of the last glaciation, when the climate was periglacial.
notes.tip: Solifluction is a slow process, like soil creep.

notes.b: Rockfall and landslide both move solid rock quickly. The difference is that rockfall is a free fall from a cliff, while a landslide is a slide along a plane.
points: Rockfall: blocks loosened by freeze-thaw, or undercut by the sea or a river (worn away at the base), fall freely from a steep cliff. They collect as scree (also called talus) at the foot.

Landslide (rockslide): a mass of rock or debris slides suddenly along a flat plane, such as a bedding plane (a layer boundary in sedimentary rock) or joint (a crack) sloping in the same direction as the slope.
Landslides often follow heavy rain, which lubricates the plane so the rock slips more easily, or an earthquake, which shakes it loose.
notes.tip: Keep landslide and slump separate. A landslide moves along a flat plane.

notes.b: A slump is a fast slide in which the moving mass turns as it goes, because the surface it slides on is curved rather than flat.
points: Saturated material, often clay over or under permeable rock (rock that lets water through), slides along a curved (concave) slip plane and rotates backward.
The slump leaves a crescent-shaped scar (scarp) at the top, a back-tilted block and a bulging toe at the foot.
Slumps are common on clay cliffs undercut by the sea, because the sea removes the support at the base, for example on the Antrim coast.
A slump moves on a curved plane. A landslide moves on a flat plane.
notes.tip: Slump is rotational, on a curved slip plane. Do not mix it up with a landslide or rockslide, which moves on a flat plane.

notes.b: These three fast flows each carry a wet or loose mass downhill: mud, volcanic mud, or snow and ice. All are triggered by a sudden supply of water or by disturbance.
points: Mudflow: fine material (clay, silt, weathered rock or volcanic ash) saturated by heavy rain or snowmelt flows rapidly downhill like a liquid, often along valleys. It can bury settlements.
Lahar: a volcanic mudflow of ash and water, from rain or from melted snow and ice on the volcano. It can travel very fast and far. The word is from Indonesia.
Avalanche: a sudden, rapid slide of snow and ice down a steep mountain slope, triggered by heavy snowfall, rapid thaw or disturbance.
Ice avalanches occur when part of a glacier collapses, such as at Marmolada in 2022.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to match photos to soil creep, rockfall, avalanche, mudflow, lahar and landslide, and to say whether each is fast or slow. Mudflow, lahar and avalanche are all fast.

notes.b: A bog burst is a fast mass movement of peat, common in the uplands of Ireland. Peat (partly rotted plant matter that builds up in waterlogged ground) on a slope fills with water and then slides.
points: Blanket bog (a thick layer of peat covering a hillside) on a slope becomes saturated after prolonged or intense rain.
The peat gains weight, and its base loses grip on the underlying mineral soil or rock. The peat bursts and flows downhill as a black slurry.
A bog burst blocks rivers, kills fish, and destroys roads, bridges and land.
Bog bursts are common in the uplands of western and north-western Ireland.
notes.tip: Bog burst is a fast process. If asked for a fast example, it is one you can back with Irish case studies.

notes.b: Whether a slope moves, and how fast, depends on a set of factors. The first three are the slope angle, the water in the ground and what the slope is made of.
points: Gradient (slope angle): the steeper the slope, the greater the downslope pull of gravity and the faster the movement. Gentle slopes favour creep; steep slopes favour falls and slides.
Water content: some water adds cohesion, but saturation fills the pores (the tiny gaps between particles), adds weight, reduces friction and acts as a lubricant, so material flows.
Heavy or prolonged rain and snowmelt trigger most fast movements, because they saturate the slope.
Clay becomes slippery and plastic (easily moulded) when wet. Jointed or bedded rock dipping towards the slope slides.
Permeable rock over impermeable clay or shale (rock that water cannot pass through) concentrates water at the junction, as on the Antrim coast.
notes.tip: You may be asked to name two factors and explain one, such as slope or water. For a 30-mark question on one process, explain each factor for that process.

notes.h: Factors: vegetation, climate, undercutting and tectonics
notes.b: The remaining factors either hold a slope together or remove what supports it. Some are natural, some come from the climate, and one is human.
points: Vegetation: roots bind soil and plants absorb water, so bare slopes move more easily.
Climate and weathering: freeze-thaw loosens rock, heavy seasonal rainfall adds water, and periglacial climates produce solifluction.
Undercutting: erosion by the sea or a river at the base of a slope removes support, so the material above is left unsupported.
Loading: extra weight at the top of a slope, from rock, buildings or spoil (waste rock), increases the downslope force.
Tectonic activity: earthquakes and volcanic eruptions shake loose material and trigger landslides and lahars.
Human activity also affects slope stability. There is more on this in Human interaction: mass movement.
notes.tip: For one process, explain gradient, water, material, vegetation, climate, undercutting and human activity, and give an example.

notes.b: The Antrim coast is an Irish example of landslides and slumps. Its layers of rock, hard on top of soft, explain why the slopes fail.
points: Location: the Antrim coast between Larne and Cushendall, along the Antrim Coast Road (A2).
Geology: hard basalt lies on chalk, which lies on soft Lias clay with other mudstones.
Rainwater soaks through the jointed basalt and chalk and saturates the clay, which becomes slippery and plastic.
The rock above slumps and rotates seaward in rotational slides, and clay flows out as mudflows. These have repeatedly blocked the coast road.
Garron Point is a classic landslip site on this coast.
Responses, so that the road stays open: engineers have built retaining walls and drainage, and fitted rock-catch fences and netting to protect the road.
notes.tip: Exams may set a news article on a landslide and ask about its cause, preparation, effects and follow-on flood risk.

notes.h: Case study: bog bursts in Ireland
notes.b: Two Irish bog bursts show how rain-soaked peat can fail, one recent and one historic.
points: Pollatomish (Dooncarton Mountain), Co. Mayo, 19 September 2003: an intense thunderstorm with very heavy rain triggered about 40 landslides and peat slides in a few hours.
At Pollatomish, houses, roads, a bridge and a graveyard were damaged, and several families were evacuated.
Knocknageeha, near Rathmore, Co. Kerry, December 1896: a bog burst swept away a house, killing a family of eight. It is the classic Irish bog burst.
notes.tip: Questions on a bog burst news article ask about cause, preparation, effects and follow-on flood risk.

notes.b: Italy gives two international examples: mudflows after heavy rain at Sarno, and a landslide into a reservoir at Vajont.
points: Sarno and neighbouring towns, Campania, southern Italy, 5-6 May 1998: after prolonged heavy rain, loose volcanic ash and soil on steep limestone slopes became saturated and slid off as fast mudflows into the towns below. About 160 people were killed.

Vajont Dam, northern Italy, 9 October 1963: a huge landslide from Monte Toc slid into the reservoir (the lake held back by the dam). The wave it sent over the dam destroyed the town of Longarone, killing about 2,000 people. The dam itself survived.
Weak clay layers in the valley side, and the filling of the reservoir which saturated the slope, caused the Vajont slide.

notes.b: South America gives a lahar triggered by a volcano and mudslides triggered by torrential rain.
points: Nevado del Ruiz, Colombia, 13 November 1985: a small eruption melted part of the summit ice cap. Lahars rushed down river valleys and buried the town of Armero, killing about 23,000 people.
Warnings had been given, but Armero was not evacuated.
Vargas state, on the coast of Venezuela, December 1999: days of torrential rain triggered mudslides and debris flows on the steep mountains above coastal towns, killing thousands of people.

notes.h: Case study: glacier collapse in the Alps
notes.b: Recent glacier collapses in the Alps are mass movements of ice, rock and mud. They show glacier retreat acting as a new cause.
points: Blatten, Lötschental, canton of Valais, Switzerland, 28 May 2025: the Birch Glacier collapsed, sending a huge mass of ice, rock and mud onto the village and burying most of it.
The village had been evacuated days earlier, after geologists detected rockfalls onto the glacier.
The debris blocked the River Lonza, forming a lake upstream, which means a flood risk.
Marmolada glacier, Dolomites, Italy, 3 July 2022: during a heatwave a large section of the glacier collapsed as an ice avalanche, killing 11 people.
notes.tip: Questions on a news article about a landslide ask about its cause, preparation, effects and follow-on flood risk.

keyTerms.definition: The downslope movement of weathered material under gravity, without a transporting agent such as a river or glacier.
The layer of loose, weathered material that covers bedrock and can be moved by mass movement.
The slowest mass movement, in which soil is lifted at right angles to the slope by wetting or frost heave and dropped vertically, moving it slowly downhill.
The slow flow of a saturated thawed surface layer over permafrost in periglacial areas.
The accumulation of rock fragments at the foot of a steep cliff after rockfall; also called talus.
A rotational slide of saturated material along a curved slip plane, leaving a crescent-shaped scarp.
The rapid downhill flow of saturated fine material that moves like a liquid.
A volcanic mudflow of ash and water, from rain or melted snow and ice on a volcano.
The sudden flow of saturated blanket peat down a slope, after its base loses grip on the mineral soil or rock beneath.
The force that holds particles of soil or rock together, resisting movement.

factCards.term: Mass movement: the forces on a slope and when material moves
factCards.definition: Gravity pulls material downslope; friction, cohesion and plant roots resist it. Movement happens when the downslope force exceeds the resistance. Weathering supplies the material, and no transporting agent is needed.

factCards.term: Mass movements: which are fast and which are slow
factCards.definition: Slow: soil creep and solifluction. Fast: rockfall, landslide, slump, mudflow, lahar, bog burst and avalanche. Movements are also classed by water content (dry or wet) and type of movement (heave, slide, flow or fall).

factCards.term: Mass movement: where and when it is most active
factCards.definition: In space: most intense on steep, wet and unvegetated slopes. In time: more frequent after heavy rain, snowmelt, earthquakes and seasonal freeze-thaw.

factCards.term: Soil creep: five pieces of evidence on a slope
factCards.definition: Terracettes (small steps on grassy slopes); bent tree trunks; tilted fences, walls and poles; soil piled up behind walls; cracked roads.

factCards.term: Rockfall: what causes it and what it leaves
factCards.definition: Blocks loosened by freeze-thaw, or undercut by the sea or a river, fall freely from a steep cliff and collect as scree (talus) at its foot.

factCards.term: Landslide vs slump: how the movement differs
factCards.definition: Landslide: rock or debris slides suddenly along a flat plane, such as a bedding plane or joint dipping with the slope. Slump: saturated material rotates backward on a curved slip plane, leaving a crescent-shaped scarp, a back-tilted block and a bulging toe.

factCards.term: Bog burst: how it happens and its effects
factCards.definition: Prolonged or intense rain saturates sloping blanket bog; the peat gains weight and its base loses grip on the mineral soil or rock below, so it bursts and flows downhill as a black slurry, blocking rivers, killing fish and wrecking roads, bridges and land.

On 19 September 2003 an intense thunderstorm with very heavy rain triggered about 40 landslides and peat slides on Dooncarton Mountain in a few hours; houses, roads, a bridge and a graveyard were damaged and several families were evacuated.

factCards.term: Knocknageeha, Co. Kerry: the classic Irish bog burst
factCards.definition: In December 1896, near Rathmore, Co. Kerry, a bog burst swept away a house, killing a family of eight.

factCards.term: Antrim coast landslides: the geology and the process
factCards.definition: Between Larne and Cushendall, hard basalt lies on chalk over soft Lias clay. Rain soaks through the jointed basalt and chalk into the clay, which turns slippery and plastic; the rock above slumps seaward in rotational slides and clay flows out as mudflows.

factCards.term: Antrim Coast Road: effects of the landslides and the responses
factCards.definition: Mudflows have repeatedly blocked the Antrim Coast Road (A2); Garron Point is a classic landslip site. Engineers have built retaining walls and drainage, and fitted rock-catch fences and netting to protect the road.

On 5–6 May 1998, after prolonged heavy rain, loose volcanic ash and soil on steep limestone slopes in Campania became saturated and slid off as fast mudflows into Sarno and neighbouring towns; about 160 people were killed.

factCards.term: Vajont Dam, Italy, 1963: what happened and why
factCards.definition: On 9 October 1963 a landslide from Monte Toc fell into the reservoir; the wave over the dam destroyed Longarone, killing about 2,000 people, though the dam survived. Causes: weak clay layers in the valley side, and filling the reservoir saturated the slope.

On 13 November 1985 a small eruption of Nevado del Ruiz melted part of its summit ice cap; lahars rushed down river valleys and buried the town of Armero, killing about 23,000 people. Warnings had been given, but the town was not evacuated.
In December 1999 days of torrential rain triggered mudslides and debris flows on the steep mountains above coastal towns in Vargas state, killing thousands of people.

On 28 May 2025 the Birch Glacier collapsed, burying most of Blatten in ice, rock and mud. Rockfalls onto the glacier had been detected, so the village was evacuated days earlier. The debris dammed the River Lonza, forming a lake upstream and a flood risk.
On 3 July 2022, during a heatwave, a large section of the Marmolada glacier in the Dolomites collapsed as an ice avalanche, killing 11 people: glacier retreat as a new cause of mass movement.

factCards.term: Mass movement factors: how gradient and water affect it
factCards.definition: The steeper the slope, the stronger the downslope pull of gravity: gentle slopes favour creep, steep slopes falls and slides. Some water adds cohesion, but saturation fills pores, adds weight, reduces friction and lubricates, so material flows.

factCards.term: Mass movement factors: rock type, vegetation, undercutting and tectonics
factCards.definition: Wet clay turns slippery and plastic, and rock dipping towards the slope slides; roots bind soil and plants absorb water, so bare slopes move more easily; erosion at the base removes support and weight at the top adds force; earthquakes shake material loose.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the factors governing the operation of one mass movement process that you have studied.
questions.model: Process: a bog burst, in which saturated blanket peat on a slope loses its grip on the mineral soil beneath and flows downhill as a slurry. Gradient: on a steep slope, gravity pulls the peat down faster, so the burst travels further. Water: intense or prolonged rain saturates the peat, fills its pores, adds weight, reduces friction and lubricates the base. At Pollatomish, Co. Mayo, on 19 September 2003, an intense thunderstorm triggered peat slides in a few hours. Material: peat has little cohesion when saturated and lies on impermeable mineral soil or rock. Vegetation: bare or drained bog has no roots to hold the peat. Climate: heavy seasonal rainfall keeps the peat saturated. Undercutting: erosion at the base of a slope removes support. Human activity: drainage or cutting of the bog weakens its surface (see the notes on Human interaction: mass movement). Example: at Knocknageeha, near Rathmore, Co. Kerry, in December 1896, a bog burst swept away a house, killing a family of eight.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain any two processes of mass movement.
questions.model: Soil creep: the slowest process, moving soil a few millimetres to centimetres a year. Wetting swells the soil and frost heave lifts particles at right angles to the slope; on drying or thawing they drop vertically, so each cycle moves them a little downslope. Evidence includes terracettes, bent tree trunks, tilted fences and walls, soil piled up behind walls, and cracked roads. Mudflow: a fast process in which fine material such as clay, silt or volcanic ash is saturated by heavy rain or snowmelt and flows downhill like a liquid, often along valleys. Water lubricates the material and reduces friction, so a steep valley side can give way suddenly. Example: at Sarno, Campania, southern Italy, in May 1998, saturated volcanic ash and soil on steep limestone slopes slid off as fast mudflows into the towns below, killing about 160 people.

questions.prompt: Name one fast and one slow type of mass movement, and explain briefly how slope affects the rate of mass movement.
questions.model: Fast: rockfall (or any one of landslide, slump, mudflow, lahar, bog burst or avalanche). Slow: soil creep (or solifluction). The steeper the slope, the greater the downslope pull of gravity, so material moves faster; gentle slopes favour slow creep, while steep slopes favour rockfalls and slides.
